questions.title: The two points on the line that are exactly three units from the origin
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 3.1 (the distance between two points in three-dimensional space)
questions.subtopic: 3.1 The distance between two points in three-dimensional space
questions.challenge_mechanism: A single fixed line is probed for the points at a prescribed distance from a point off it, so the second solution sits beyond the segment the earlier parts have made familiar.
questions.question: The points $A(1,0,2)$, $B(3,4,0)$ and $C(5,8,-2)$ are given, and $O$ denotes the origin. Each part below refers to these three points and to the vectors that join them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the points $A(1,0,2)$, $B(3,4,0)$ and $C(5,8,-2)$ are collinear.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the distance $AC$, giving your answer in the form $k\sqrt{6}$ where $k$ is a positive integer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the point $P$ on the segment $AC$ such that $AP:PC=1:3$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the coordinates of the two points on the line through $A$ and $C$ whose distance from the origin is exactly three units.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The vector $\overrightarrow{AB}=(3-1,4-0,0-2)=(2,4,-2)$ **(M1)** and $\overrightarrow{BC}=(5-3,8-4,-2-0)=(2,4,-2)$ **(A1)**. The two vectors are equal, so the segments $AB$ and $BC$ are parallel **(R1)**. Since they also share the point $B$, the three points must lie on one straight line **(A1)(AG)**. Equal displacement vectors force $A$, $B$ and $C$ onto a single line, and no other arrangement of the points is consistent with the two vectors just found.

**(b)** The vector $\overrightarrow{AC}=(5-1,8-0,-2-2)=(4,8,-4)$ **(M1)**. By the distance formula, $AC=\sqrt{4^{2}+8^{2}+(-4)^{2}}$ **(M1)** $=\sqrt{16+64+16}=\sqrt{96}$ **(A1)** $=4\sqrt{6}$ **(A1)**, so $k=4$. The factor $16$ inside the root is what produces the exact surd form rather than a decimal. The distance formula used here is simply the three-dimensional form of Pythagoras applied to the three coordinate differences.

**(c)** Since $AP:PC=1:3$, the point $P$ divides $AC$ internally in that ratio, so $P=A+\frac{1}{4}(C-A)$ **(M1)**. Now $\frac{1}{4}(C-A)=\frac{1}{4}(4,8,-4)=(1,2,-1)$ **(A1)**, hence $P=(1,0,2)+(1,2,-1)$ **(A1)** $=(2,2,1)$ **(A1)**. The ratio places $P$ one quarter of the way from $A$ towards $C$. The fraction multiplies the whole vector $C-A$, so reversing the ratio would place the point three quarters of the way along instead.

**(d)** A general point of the line is $(1+4t,8t,2-4t)$ **(M1)**. Its squared distance from $O$ is $(1+4t)^{2}+(8t)^{2}+(2-4t)^{2}$ **(M1)** $=96t^{2}-8t+5$ **(A1)**. Setting this equal to $9$ gives $96t^{2}-8t-4=0$, that is $24t^{2}-2t-1=0$ **(M1)**, so $t=\frac{1}{4}$ or $t=-\frac{1}{6}$ **(A1)**. The two points are therefore $(2,2,1)$ and $\left(\frac{1}{3},-\frac{4}{3},\frac{8}{3}\right)$ **(A1)**; the first of these is exactly the point $P$ found in part (c) **(R1)**. The negative root describes the point reached by travelling in the opposite direction from $A$, away from $C$, and it lies on the same infinite line.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The (M1) is for forming at least one of the vectors $\overrightarrow{AB}$ or $\overrightarrow{BC}$; the (A1) requires both vectors correct. The (R1) is the reasoning mark: candidates must state that equal vectors have the same direction and that the points share $B$, so a candidate who computes both vectors but draws no collinearity conclusion forfeits it. The (AG) confirms the printed result.

(b) Award (M1) for the vector $\overrightarrow{AC}$ and (M1) for the distance formula. The two (A1) marks are independent: one for reaching $\sqrt{96}$, one for the exact surd form $4\sqrt{6}$. Do not accept a decimal such as $9.798$.

(c) The (M1) is for the section formula in any correct form. A candidate who uses $\frac{3}{4}A+\frac{1}{4}C$ earns full credit. Accept the coordinates in any order provided they are clearly labelled.

(d) This is the discriminating part. The (M1) is for parametrising the line, and the second (M1) for forming the squared distance. The (A1) for the quadratic $24t^{2}-2t-1=0$ may be awarded for any equivalent form. Both values of $t$ are required for the (A1), and both points for the final (A1). The (R1) recognises that $(2,2,1)$ coincides with $P$; follow through from an incorrect $P$ is allowed.
questions.explanation:
The first three parts are deliberately gentle so that the final part can carry the difficulty. Parts (a) and (b) ask for collinearity and a distance, which most candidates can do, and part (c) introduces the point $P$ that will reappear at the end. The lever is the final part: the line is fixed by $A$ and $C$, and the question asks for the points on that line at a given distance from a point that does not lie on it. Candidates who try to solve this by inspection or by drawing will not find the second point.

The natural route is to parametrise the line as $A+t(C-A)=(1+4t,8t,2-4t)$ and then impose $|OP|^{2}=9$. Expanding gives the quadratic $96t^{2}-8t+5$, and setting it equal to $9$ gives $24t^{2}-2t-1=0$, whose roots are $t=\frac{1}{4}$ and $t=-\frac{1}{6}$. The two roots correspond to the two points, one lying between $A$ and $C$ and one beyond $A$ on the other side. A candidate who assumes the answer lies on the segment $AC$ will find only $(2,2,1)$ and lose the final marks.

The most common error is to set the distance rather than the squared distance equal to $9$, which introduces a square root and hides the quadratic. Another is to use a parameter measured from $O$ instead of along $AC$. The appearance of $P$ as one of the two solutions is the intended check: it confirms that the algebra is consistent with part (c) and rewards candidates who notice the connection rather than treating the parts as unrelated. A candidate who has met only two-dimensional coordinate geometry will find the arithmetic familiar, but the extra coordinate is what makes the parametrisation of the line the natural tool rather than a sketch.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 3.1 bullet on the distance between two points in three-dimensional space. The lever is a point on the fixed line AC sought at a fixed distance from the origin rather than from a point on the line itself; the coordinates A(1,0,2), B(3,4,0) and C(5,8,-2) were chosen so that AB and BC are the identical vector (2,4,-2), making collinearity exact, and so that the distance condition reduces to 24t^2 - 2t - 1 = 0 with the clean roots t = 1/4 and t = -1/6, one of which reproduces the section point from part (c).

verification.method: Every value was recomputed in Python: the vectors AB, BC and AC, the distance sqrt(96) = 4 sqrt 6, the section point, and both roots of 96t^2 - 8t - 4 = 0 were checked against the squared-distance condition.

questions.title: The triangle the data allow twice
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 3.2 (use of the sine, cosine and tangent ratios to find the sides and angles of right-angled triangles) and SL 3.3 (applications of right and non-right angled trigonometry, including the sine rule and the ambiguous case)
questions.subtopic: 3.2 Sine, cosine and tangent ratios in right-angled triangles and 3.3 Applications of right and non-right angled trigonometry
questions.challenge_mechanism: One set of measurements admits two genuinely different triangles, and every later part must be carried through both branches rather than resolved to a single case.
questions.question: In triangle $ABC$, the side $AB$ has length $6$ cm, the side $BC$ has length $2\sqrt{3}$ cm, and the angle $BAC$ is $30^{\circ}$. The remaining angles and sides are not yet known.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that there are two possible values of angle $BCA$, and find both of them.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the two possible values of angle $ABC$, giving each of them in degrees.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the two possible lengths of $CA$, giving each answer in the form $k\sqrt{3}$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the area of each triangle, and explain which one a student who assumes the triangle is right-angled would find.

questions.answer:
**(a)** By the sine rule, $\frac{BC}{\sin BAC}=\frac{AB}{\sin BCA}$ **(M1)**, so $\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{\sin 30^{\circ}}=\frac{6}{\sin BCA}$ **(A1)**. Since $\sin 30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{2}$, the left-hand side is $4\sqrt{3}$, giving $\sin BCA=\frac{6}{4\sqrt{3}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ **(A1)**. Hence angle $BCA=60^{\circ}$ or $120^{\circ}$ **(A1)(AG)**. Both values are admissible, because with angle $BAC=30^{\circ}$ each one leaves a positive third angle. The equation $\sin BCA=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ is the crucial step, because the sine function takes the same value at two different angles in the range from $0^{\circ}$ to $180^{\circ}$.

**(b)** The angle sum gives $ABC=180^{\circ}-30^{\circ}-BCA$ **(M1)**. For $BCA=60^{\circ}$ this is $90^{\circ}$ **(A1)**, and for $BCA=120^{\circ}$ it is $30^{\circ}$ **(A1)**. Both values are positive, so both triangles exist **(R1)**. The two third angles come from the same angle-sum relation, and neither is negative, which is the test that decides whether a candidate angle is admissible.

**(c)** Again by the sine rule, $\frac{CA}{\sin ABC}=4\sqrt{3}$ **(M1)**, so $CA=4\sqrt{3}\sin ABC$ **(A1)**. When $ABC=90^{\circ}$, $CA=4\sqrt{3}$ cm **(A1)**; when $ABC=30^{\circ}$, $CA=4\sqrt{3}\cdot\frac{1}{2}=2\sqrt{3}$ cm **(A1)**. The length of $CA$ depends on the angle opposite it, so the two possible values of angle $ABC$ produce two different lengths rather than one.

**(d)** The area is $\frac{1}{2}(AB)(BC)\sin ABC$ **(M1)** $=\frac{1}{2}(6)(2\sqrt{3})\sin ABC=6\sqrt{3}\sin ABC$ **(A1)**. For $ABC=90^{\circ}$ this is $6\sqrt{3}$ cm$^{2}$ **(A1)**, and for $ABC=30^{\circ}$ it is $6\sqrt{3}\cdot\frac{1}{2}=3\sqrt{3}$ cm$^{2}$ **(A1)**. A candidate who assumes the triangle is right-angled obtains only the first value and never sees the obtuse case at all **(R1)**. The area formula uses the two given sides and the angle between them, so it changes with the angle even though the sides themselves are fixed.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The (M1) is for the sine rule with the given sides and angle; the (A1) for substituting $AB=6$, $BC=2\sqrt{3}$ and $\sin 30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{2}$. The third (A1) is for the exact value $\sin BCA=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, and the final (A1) requires both angles. A candidate who gives only $60^{\circ}$ forfeits the last mark but keeps the rest.

(b) Award (M1) for using the angle sum; the two (A1) marks are independent, one for each value of angle $ABC$. The (R1) requires the candidate to state that both third angles are positive, which is what makes both triangles admissible.

(c) The (M1) is for identifying the sine-rule constant $4\sqrt{3}$; the (A1) is for the general expression $CA=4\sqrt{3}\sin ABC$. The two (A1) marks are for the two lengths, which must be exact surds. Accept $2\sqrt{3}$ and $4\sqrt{3}$ in either order provided they are correctly matched to their angles.

(d) The (M1) is for the area formula using two sides and the included angle; the (A1) for the factorised expression $6\sqrt{3}\sin ABC$. Each area carries its own (A1). The final (R1) is a reasoning mark for explaining that the right-angled assumption discards the obtuse triangle, and it is not awarded for a bare statement of the larger area.
questions.explanation:
This item is built on the ambiguous case of the sine rule, and the ambiguity is genuine rather than decorative. The data are one side, a second side and a non-included angle, exactly the configuration in which two triangles can satisfy the same three measurements. The value $\sin BCA=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ has two solutions in the interval from $0^{\circ}$ to $180^{\circ}$, namely $60^{\circ}$ and $120^{\circ}$, and both must be tested against the angle sum rather than discarded automatically.

The common error is to assume that the larger angle is impossible. Candidates who have memorised that a triangle cannot contain two obtuse angles sometimes reject $120^{\circ}$ without checking the sum. Here $30^{\circ}+120^{\circ}=150^{\circ}$, so the third angle is $30^{\circ}$ and the triangle is perfectly valid. The other error is the reverse: to accept only the acute solution because it is the one the calculator returns, since the inverse sine reports $60^{\circ}$ and hides $120^{\circ}$.

Part (d) gives the ambiguity a consequence. The two triangles have areas $6\sqrt{3}$ and $3\sqrt{3}$, and a candidate who silently assumes a right angle obtains only the larger one. The lever is therefore not the sine rule itself, which is routine, but the requirement to keep both branches alive through four linked parts and then to explain what is lost by collapsing them. The side $BC=2\sqrt{3}$ was chosen so that the sine-rule constant is the clean value $4\sqrt{3}$ and both lengths and both areas come out as exact multiples of $\sqrt{3}$. A sketch of both triangles, one with a right angle at $B$ and one with an obtuse angle at $C$, makes the two cases visually distinct. The final part asks what is lost when the right angle is assumed silently.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 3.2 and SL 3.3 bullets on the sine rule and the ambiguous case. The lever is the non-included angle: AB = 6, BC = 2 sqrt 3 and angle BAC = 30 degrees were chosen so that sin(BCA) = sqrt 3 / 2 exactly, producing the two admissible angles 60 and 120 degrees, and so that the two resulting areas 6 sqrt 3 and 3 sqrt 3 differ by a clean factor of two. The item is not a reskin because the ambiguity is carried through four linked parts and made the object of the final explanation rather than being dismissed in a single line.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed in Python: the sine-rule constant 4 sqrt 3, both angles from sin(BCA) = sqrt 3 / 2, both third angles, both lengths of CA and both areas were checked, together with the cosine-rule confirmation CA^2 = 48 and 12.

questions.title: An area that fixes the sine but not the angle
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 3.3 (applications of right and non-right angled trigonometry: the sine rule, the cosine rule and the area of a triangle)
questions.subtopic: 3.3 Applications of right and non-right angled trigonometry
questions.challenge_mechanism: The given area pins down the sine of the included angle but not the sign of its cosine, so two triangles survive until a later measurement separates them.
questions.question: In triangle $PQR$, the side $PQ$ has length $7$ cm, the side $QR$ has length $15$ cm, and the area of the triangle is $42$ cm$^{2}$. A calculator is permitted throughout this question.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that $\sin Q=0.8$, and write down the two possible values of angle $PQR$ correct to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the two possible values of $PR$, giving one of them as an exact surd and one as an integer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the perimeter of each triangle, and state which of the two is obtuse-angled.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the area alone does not determine the triangle, and state one further measurement that would.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The area of a triangle is $\frac{1}{2}(PQ)(QR)\sin Q$ **(M1)**, so $\frac{1}{2}(7)(15)\sin Q=42$ **(A1)**. Since $\frac{1}{2}(7)(15)=52.5$, this gives $\sin Q=\frac{42}{52.5}=0.8$ **(A1)(AG)**. Hence angle $PQR=53.1^{\circ}$ or $126.9^{\circ}$, correct to one decimal place **(A1)**. The area formula is the only relation that uses the given quantity directly, and it is the reason the sine of the angle, rather than the angle itself, is what the data determine.

**(b)** By the cosine rule, $PR^{2}=PQ^{2}+QR^{2}-2(PQ)(QR)\cos Q$ **(M1)** $=7^{2}+15^{2}-210\cos Q=274-210\cos Q$ **(A1)**. For $Q=53.1^{\circ}$ we have $\cos Q=0.6$, so $PR^{2}=274-126=148$ and $PR=2\sqrt{37}$ cm **(M1)(A1)**. For $Q=126.9^{\circ}$ we have $\cos Q=-0.6$, so $PR^{2}=274+126=400$ and $PR=20$ cm **(A1)**. The cosine rule is applied twice, once with the positive cosine and once with the negative, because the two cases differ only in the sign of $\cos Q$.

**(c)** The first perimeter is $7+15+2\sqrt{37}=34.2$ cm to three significant figures **(M1)(A1)**. The second perimeter is $7+15+20=42$ cm **(A1)**. The second triangle is obtuse-angled, because angle $PQR=126.9^{\circ}$ is greater than $90^{\circ}$ **(R1)**. The perimeters differ by almost eight centimetres, which is a useful reminder that equal areas do not imply congruent triangles.

**(d)** The area fixes only $\sin Q$, and $\sin Q=\sin(180^{\circ}-Q)$, so an acute angle and its supplement produce the same area while giving two different triangles **(M1)(A1)**. One further measurement would remove the ambiguity: whether angle $PQR$ is acute or obtuse, the length of $PR$, or the size of either of the remaining angles **(A1)**. The ambiguity is a feature of the sine function rather than of the triangle, and it disappears as soon as any measurement that distinguishes an angle from its supplement is supplied.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The (M1) is for the area formula with two sides and the included angle; the (A1) for the correct substitution. The (A1) requires the exact value $0.8$, and the final (A1) both angles to one decimal place. A candidate who writes only $53.1^{\circ}$ earns three of the four marks, because the supplement is the point of the question.

(b) Award (M1) for the cosine rule and (A1) for the reduced expression $274-210\cos Q$. The (M1)(A1) pair is for the acute case, including the exact surd $2\sqrt{37}$; a decimal such as $12.2$ does not earn the surd mark. The final (A1) is for $PR=20$ in the obtuse case. Accept the two answers in either order if they are correctly matched to their angles.

(c) The (M1) is for adding the three sides; the first (A1) is for the perimeter $34.2$ cm to three significant figures, and the second for $42$ cm. The (R1) requires an explicit comparison of $126.9^{\circ}$ with $90^{\circ}$; stating only that the second triangle is larger does not earn it.

(d) This is a reasoning part. Award (M1) for the identity $\sin Q=\sin(180^{\circ}-Q)$ or an equivalent statement about the area, (A1) for linking it to the two triangles, and the final (A1) for any one valid extra measurement. Follow through from part (a) is allowed.
questions.explanation:
The item is built around a quantity that is not determined by the information given. Two sides and the area fix $\sin Q$, but $\sin Q$ is the same for an acute angle and its supplement, so the data are consistent with two triangles of equal area. The cosine rule then separates them, because $\cos Q$ changes sign between the two cases: one triangle has $PR=2\sqrt{37}$, and the other has $PR=20$.

Candidates who use the cosine rule without thinking about the sign of $\cos Q$ will obtain only one value. If they assume the acute angle, they compute $274-126=148$; if they assume the obtuse angle, they compute $274+126=400$. Both are correct, but each belongs to a different triangle. The trap is to treat the second as an error rather than as the second branch.

Part (c) makes the distinction concrete through the perimeters, and the obtuse triangle is identified by the size of angle $Q$ rather than by any feature of the sides alone. Part (d) steps back and asks why the ambiguity arises in the first place; the answer is the symmetry $\sin Q=\sin(180^{\circ}-Q)$, which is also the reason the sine rule has an ambiguous case. The numbers $7$, $15$ and $42$ were chosen so that $\sin Q=0.8$ exactly and so that the two squared lengths are $148$ and $400$, the first reducing to $2\sqrt{37}$ and the second to a whole number. A candidate who checks $\cos^{2}Q+\sin^{2}Q=0.36+0.64=1$ will confirm that both branches correspond to genuine angles. The two triangles share the same two sides and the same area, so no measurement of area can ever separate them; only a measurement sensitive to the size of the angle can. It is the same ambiguity that appears in the ambiguous case of the sine rule.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 3.3 bullet on the cosine rule and the area of a triangle. The lever is the reversal of the usual flow: here the area is given and the included angle is unknown, so the area fixes sin Q = 0.8 rather than an angle; PQ = 7, QR = 15 and area 42 were chosen so that sin Q is exact, so that cos Q = +/-0.6, and so that the two possible third sides are the surd 2 sqrt 37 and the integer 20. The item is not a reskin because it asks for both branches and then makes the incompleteness of the area the explicit subject of the final part.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed in Python: sin Q = 42/52.5 = 0.8, the two angles via arccos(+/-0.6), both values of PR^2 = 274 -/+ 126, the perimeters and the identity cos^2 Q + sin^2 Q = 1.

questions.title: The sector whose second radius cannot exist
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 3.4 (the circle: radian measure of angles, length of an arc and area of a sector)
questions.subtopic: 3.4 The circle: radian measure of angles, length of an arc and area of a sector
questions.challenge_mechanism: Two radii satisfy the same area equation, but the larger root forces an angle beyond a full turn, so the geometry silently removes one algebraic solution.
questions.question: A sector of a circle has radius $r$ cm and angle $\theta$ radians, and its perimeter is $20$ cm. All angles in this question are to be given in radians.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the area $A$ cm$^{2}$ of the sector is given by $A=10r-r^{2}$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the value of $r$ for which $A$ is greatest, and state the greatest value of $A$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find, for $r=5$, the value of $\theta$ in radians and the length of the arc.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the two values of $r$ for which $A=16$, and explain why only one of them is possible.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The perimeter of the sector is $2r+r\theta=20$ **(M1)**, so $r\theta=20-2r$ **(A1)**. The area is $A=\frac{1}{2}r^{2}\theta=\frac{1}{2}r(r\theta)$ **(M1)** $=\frac{1}{2}r(20-2r)=10r-r^{2}$ **(A1)(AG)**. Writing the area this way removes $\theta$ entirely and leaves a single-variable expression. The substitution is the whole idea of the first part: once the angle has been eliminated, the problem becomes a question about a single variable, and the fixed perimeter is the constraint that makes the elimination possible.

**(b)** Completing the square, $A=10r-r^{2}=25-(r-5)^{2}$ **(M1)(A1)**. Since $(r-5)^{2}\ge 0$, the area is greatest when $r=5$ **(A1)**, and the greatest value is $A=25$ cm$^{2}$ **(A1)**. The value $r=5$ gives a genuine maximum rather than a minimum because the coefficient of $r^{2}$ is negative, so the parabola opens downwards. Completing the square is preferred to differentiation here because it displays the maximum and the value at which it occurs at the same time.

**(c)** Substituting $r=5$ into $r\theta=20-2r$ gives $5\theta=10$ **(M1)**, so $\theta=2$ radians **(A1)**. The arc length is $r\theta=5\cdot 2=10$ cm **(M1)(A1)**. The angle of two radians is slightly less than a third of a full turn, and the arc length of ten centimetres is exactly half the fixed perimeter.

**(d)** Setting $10r-r^{2}=16$ gives $r^{2}-10r+16=0$ **(M1)**, so $(r-2)(r-8)=0$ and $r=2$ or $r=8$ **(A1)**. For $r=2$ the angle would be $\theta=\frac{20-4}{2}=8$ radians **(A1)**, which exceeds $2\pi\approx 6.28$, so no such sector exists. For $r=8$ the angle is $\theta=\frac{20-16}{8}=0.5$ radians, which is admissible **(R1)**, so only $r=8$ survives. The two roots are found by factorising, which is straightforward because their sum is ten and their product is sixteen. Only the geometric constraint removes the smaller one.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The (M1) is for the perimeter $2r+r\theta$; the (A1) for solving it as $r\theta=20-2r$. The second (M1) is for writing the area as $\frac{1}{2}r(r\theta)$ and substituting, and the (A1) for reaching the printed form. Candidates who use $A=\frac{1}{2}r^{2}\theta$ and substitute $\theta=\frac{20-2r}{r}$ earn the same marks.

(b) Award (M1) for completing the square, or for differentiating $10-2r$ and setting the derivative to zero, and (A1) for the completed-square form. The maximum requires the value $r=5$ and the value $25$; each carries its own (A1). Accept $A\le 25$ stated as the greatest area.

(c) The (M1) is for substituting $r=5$ into the perimeter relation; the (A1) is for $\theta=2$. The arc-length marks are independent: (M1) for using $r\theta$ and (A1) for $10$ cm. Do not accept $2^{\circ}$ or any other degree measure.

(d) The (M1) is for forming the quadratic and the (A1) for both roots. The third (A1) is for computing the angle $8$ radians, and the (R1) is for rejecting it because it exceeds $2\pi$. A candidate who rejects $r=2$ without computing the angle earns at most two of the four marks. Follow through from an incorrect quadratic is allowed provided the rejection argument is sound.
questions.explanation:
The sector is a standard optimisation, but the final part turns it into a question about which of two algebraic solutions is geometrically real. The perimeter is fixed at $20$ cm, so the radius and the angle are linked by $r\theta=20-2r$; the area then becomes the one-variable quadratic $10r-r^{2}$, whose maximum is $25$ cm$^{2}$ at $r=5$. Parts (a) to (c) are there to make that reduction explicit and to give the reader the tools needed for the last part.

The twist is that $A=16$ has two algebraic solutions, $r=2$ and $r=8$, but only one of them corresponds to a sector. The angle for $r=2$ is $\theta=8$ radians, which is larger than $2\pi$, and an angle greater than a full turn does not describe a simple sector. The angle for $r=8$ is $0.5$ radians, which is perfectly possible. The condition that must be checked is therefore $\theta\le 2\pi$, or equivalently $r\ge\frac{20}{2+2\pi}$, and it is not visible in the quadratic itself.

Candidates who stop at the two roots will report both and lose the reasoning mark. The same check explains why the maximum at $r=5$ gives $\theta=2$ radians, comfortably within range. A useful sanity check is to substitute each radius back into the perimeter: $2(2)+2(8)=20$ and $2(8)+8(0.5)=20$ both hold, so the perimeter alone cannot distinguish the two cases; only the constraint on the angle can. The numbers $20$, $16$ and the radius $5$ were chosen so that the quadratic factors over the integers and the maximum is exact. The maximum area of twenty-five square centimetres occurs at a radius of five centimetres, which is exactly a quarter of the fixed perimeter. The angle constraint is easy to forget in a purely algebraic treatment.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 3.4 bullet on radian measure, arc length and sector area. The lever is a fixed perimeter of 20 cm, which makes the area the quadratic 10r - r^2 and turns the request A = 16 into two roots, r = 2 and r = 8; those values were chosen so that one angle is 8 radians, exceeding 2 pi, while the other is 0.5 radians, so the item tests whether the candidate checks that the angle is a genuine sector angle. It is not a reskin because the algebraic solution is deliberately over-complete and the geometry is what prunes it.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed in Python: the perimeter relation for r = 2, 5 and 8, the areas 16, 25 and 16, the angles 8, 2 and 0.5 radians, the discriminant 36 and the inequalities 8 > 2 pi and 0.5 < 2 pi.

questions.title: Two solutions in one period, ten in five
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 3.5 (definition of cos theta and sin theta in terms of the unit circle) and SL 3.6 (the Pythagorean identity cos^2 theta + sin^2 theta = 1) and SL 3.7 (the circular functions sin x, cos x and tan x: their domains, ranges and periodicity) and SL 3.8 (solving trigonometric equations in a finite interval)
questions.subtopic: 3.5 The unit circle and 3.6 The Pythagorean identity and 3.7 The circular functions and 3.8 Solving trigonometric equations
questions.challenge_mechanism: Two sign conditions pin the angle to a single quadrant, and the later parts force its squared identities and its periodic solutions to be handled without ever recomputing the angle.
questions.question: The angle $\theta$ satisfies $\sin\theta=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $\cos\theta<0$. All angles in this question are measured in radians.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the exact values of $\cos\theta$ and of $\tan\theta$, giving each as a simplified fraction or surd.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that $(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)^{2}+(\sin\theta-\cos\theta)^{2}=2$ for every value of the angle $\theta$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the exact value of $\sin\theta\cos\theta$, and hence find the exact value of $\sin^{4}\theta+\cos^{4}\theta$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Solve $\sin x=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ for $x$ in the interval $[0,2\pi)$, and hence state the number of solutions in $[0,10\pi)$.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Since $\sin\theta=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ is negative and $\cos\theta<0$, the angle $\theta$ lies in the third quadrant **(M1)**. The Pythagorean identity gives $\cos^{2}\theta=1-\sin^{2}\theta=1-\frac{3}{4}=\frac{1}{4}$, so $\cos\theta=\pm\frac{1}{2}$ **(A1)**; the third-quadrant condition selects $\cos\theta=-\frac{1}{2}$. Therefore $\tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=\frac{-\sqrt{3}/2}{-1/2}=\sqrt{3}$ **(A1)**.

**(b)** Expanding, $(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)^{2}=\sin^{2}\theta+2\sin\theta\cos\theta+\cos^{2}\theta$ and $(\sin\theta-\cos\theta)^{2}=\sin^{2}\theta-2\sin\theta\cos\theta+\cos^{2}\theta$ **(M1)**. Adding the two expressions, the cross terms $+2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ and $-2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ cancel **(A1)**, leaving $2\sin^{2}\theta+2\cos^{2}\theta=2(\sin^{2}\theta+\cos^{2}\theta)$ **(A1)** $=2$ **(AG)**. The identity holds for every angle because it never uses the particular values from part (a); the cross terms cancel in exactly the same way in every quadrant.

**(c)** From part (a), $\sin\theta\cos\theta=\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$ **(M1)(A1)**. For the fourth powers, write $\sin^{4}\theta+\cos^{4}\theta=(\sin^{2}\theta+\cos^{2}\theta)^{2}-2\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta$ **(M1)**. The first bracket equals $1$, and $\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta=\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\right)^{2}=\frac{3}{16}$ **(A1)**, so the expression is $1-2\cdot\frac{3}{16}=1-\frac{3}{8}=\frac{5}{8}$ **(A1)**. This identity is the standard companion of the Pythagorean relation.

**(d)** In the interval $[0,2\pi)$ the equation $\sin x=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ has one solution in the third quadrant and one in the fourth **(M1)**. The reference angle is $\frac{\pi}{3}$, so the solutions are $x=\pi+\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{4\pi}{3}$ **(A1)** and $x=2\pi-\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{5\pi}{3}$ **(A1)**. Since $\sin x$ has period $2\pi$, the interval $[0,10\pi)$ contains $\frac{10\pi}{2\pi}=5$ complete periods **(M1)**, and each contributes two solutions, giving $2\times 5=10$ solutions in total **(A1)**.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The (M1) is for locating the angle in the third quadrant from the two sign conditions. The (A1) is for $\cos^{2}\theta=\frac{1}{4}$ and the second (A1) for selecting the negative root; a candidate who gives $+\frac{1}{2}$ forfeits the second mark.

(b) The marks are for structure. The (M1) is for expanding at least one square correctly; the (A1) is for the cancellation of the cross terms; the final (A1) requires the explicit use of $\sin^{2}\theta+\cos^{2}\theta=1$. A candidate who substitutes the numerical values from part (a) instead of proving the identity earns no marks here.

(c) The (M1)(A1) pair is for $\sin\theta\cos\theta=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$; accept a direct product from part (a). The second (M1) is for the identity $\sin^{4}\theta+\cos^{4}\theta=1-2\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta$, and the final (A1) is for $\frac{5}{8}$. Follow through from an incorrect product is allowed.

(d) Award (M1) for identifying the two quadrants and (A1) for each exact solution. The final marks require the count of five periods and the product $2\times 5=10$; a candidate who lists the ten solutions explicitly earns full credit. Do not accept $x=\frac{\pi}{3}$ or $x=\frac{2\pi}{3}$, which solve the equation with the positive value $+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.
questions.explanation:
The item links four syllabus bullets around a single angle. The angle is fixed by two sign conditions, $\sin\theta<0$ and $\cos\theta<0$, which together place it in the third quadrant and determine $\cos\theta$ and $\tan\theta$ without any ambiguity. Parts (b) and (c) then test whether the candidate can move between the squared identities and the values themselves, rather than treating the angle as a black box.

Part (b) is a proof that should be done symbolically. Substituting the numbers from part (a) is tempting because they are available, but it does not establish the identity for every $\theta$ and earns nothing. The cross terms $+2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ and $-2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ are the whole content of the proof, and recognising that they cancel is the point.

Part (c) is where the two threads meet. The product $\sin\theta\cos\theta=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$ comes from the values in part (a), and the identity $\sin^{4}\theta+\cos^{4}\theta=(\sin^{2}\theta+\cos^{2}\theta)^{2}-2\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta$ converts the fourth powers into that product. Candidates who try to compute $\sin^{4}\theta$ and $\cos^{4}\theta$ separately make heavy work of a simple substitution.

Part (d) moves to the general solution and asks for a count over five periods. The two solutions in $[0,2\pi)$ are $\frac{4\pi}{3}$ and $\frac{5\pi}{3}$, and periodicity multiplies them by five. The common error is to use the positive value $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and obtain $\frac{\pi}{3}$ and $\frac{2\pi}{3}$, which satisfy the wrong equation. The value $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ was chosen so that the reference angle is $\frac{\pi}{3}$ and every solution is an exact multiple of $\frac{\pi}{3}$. A candidate who counts the periods carefully will see that the count depends only on the number of complete periods in the interval, not on the particular value of the sine.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 3.5 to 3.8 bullets on the unit circle, the Pythagorean identity, the circular functions and solving trigonometric equations in a finite interval. The lever is a pair of sign conditions, sin theta < 0 and cos theta < 0, that selects one of the two angles with sin theta = -sqrt 3 / 2 and therefore makes cos theta = -1/2 and tan theta = sqrt 3 unique; the value sqrt 3 / 2 was chosen so that sin^4 theta + cos^4 theta collapses to 5/8 and so that the solutions in [0, 2 pi) are the exact multiples 4 pi / 3 and 5 pi / 3, giving ten solutions over five periods.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed in Python: sin, cos and tan at 4 pi / 3 and 5 pi / 3, the identities (sin + cos)^2 + (sin - cos)^2 = 2 and sin^4 + cos^4 = 5/8, the product sqrt 3 / 4 and the period count 10 pi / (2 pi) = 5.
